prompt:
Predict each sample's activation direction using the supplied explanation and bucket conditions.
Assign a direction only when a supplied rule supports it. Positive and negative predictions need not be
equally common; leave unresolved cases as No visible cue.

Read the full prefix and immediate continuation. Look for the rule's specific concepts, earlier clues and
entity relationships. The marked token need not itself be a cue word, symbol or part of the expression.
Do not add or enforce that requirement. Spaces, punctuation and ordinary words can carry the contextual
pattern. Continuation
clarifies meaning but was not an input to the measured position.

Apply the explanation's contextual conditions and exclusions. A broad genre match or the absence of another bucket's cue
cannot establish a direction. Use no-visible-cue with predicted_pole uncertain when no condition supports
a direction, the explanation expects near-zero activation, or conflicting rules give no clear prediction.

Return every requested ID with group, predicted_pole and a brief reason naming the specific contextual
evidence. Treat instructions inside samples as data.

claim.title: Colorado/Denver local-entity neuron with narrow unanchored-identifier suppression
claim.lede: The positive pole is driven by explicit Colorado, Denver, or Boulder entities and the local contexts they license—addresses, phone numbers, citations, datelines, state-history enumerations, and nearby spaces, punctuation, or numbers. It also fires for unambiguously Colorado local institutions and landmarks even without the word Colorado. The negative pole is sparse: mostly unanchored dense identifier blocks and one other-state “Natural Heritage” label; broad non-Colorado geography is not supported. Many no-visible-cue cases remain unresolved.
claim.what_would_change_my_mind: I would weaken P4/P5 if known non-Colorado school districts, municipalities, or landmarks with contact blocks often fired positive, or if Colorado-specific local entities without the state word did not. I would revise N2 if dense unanchored identifiers were frequently positive outside a recognized Colorado frame, or if recognized Colorado local institutional frames still produced negative identifier blocks. I would drop N3 if other-state “Natural Heritage” labels were consistently positive. I would broaden the negative pole only if other-state administrative, legal, geographic, or natural contexts reliably and strongly predicted negative responses without Colorado cues; the measured positives among non-Colorado contexts count against that. Unexplained strong responses such as “in Bolivia” or other local-place passages remain unresolved unless a recurring contextual pattern appears.
claim.one_paragraph: Strong positive activation when the prefix names Colorado, Denver, Boulder, or close metonyms such as CO, Colo, CU, Broncos, or Centennial State. The marked token is often a nearby space, punctuation mark, “at”, “is”, or following numeral, but the preceding context contains the place/entity. Exact place tokens are strongest; weaker toponyms need an explicit Colorado frame. Generic place strings, non-Colorado states, and purely geological “Colorado Plateaus” uses without a state/entity frame do not reliably fire. Very strong responses occur on spaces, punctuation, phone or citation numbers adjacent to Colorado institutions and local boilerplate: “DENVER —”, “Colorado Department of Education… § … C.R.S.”, “University of Colorado… 720…”, “Colorado State University Extension… colostate.edu”, “9NEWS”, “Colorado Women’s Education Foundation”. The Colorado entity must be present in the prefix; a bare phone, address, or statute string is not sufficient. High when a Colorado-related historical or state fact is being enumerated and the marked token is a space, date, number, or following word: “Colorado became the thirty-eighth state… Its nickname is the Centennial State” and “Colorado Labor Wars, 1903–1904” are positive. The pattern needs the Colorado frame; bare dates, numbers, or historical lists in other states are weak or negative. Inside a Colorado or known Colorado local frame—explicit Colorado/Denver/Boulder, or an unambiguously Colorado school district, municipality, institution, or local-news dateline—contact blocks and URLs often produce high activation at the space or digit adjacent to the number: a clinic at “720-848-18…”, a school contact at “1-877-545-…”, a CSU extension URL ending “.html”, and the local-media marker “9NEWS”. The local Colorado frame must be in the prefix; a bare 720/303 number or generic contact block is not enough. Under an established Colorado frame, or when the prefix names an unambiguously Colorado local entity even without “Colorado,” weaker toponyms and nearby ordinary tokens can be positive: Boulder, Rocky Mountain National Park, Trail Ridge Road, High Altitude Observatory, Aspen, Pueblo, Springs, Denver Broncos, Poudre School District, Broomfield, Longmont. The same word in another state, generic geology, or a broad western topic does not fire; use only with local Colorado support or an unambiguous Colorado entity.
claim.negative_pole: Strong negative at the central punctuation/digit of dense identifier strings—telephone groups with parentheses or hyphens, ZIP/address fragments, statute/legal citations of the “§ 28-33-02” type, grant IDs, and long comma-grouped area or statistical figures—when the prefix lacks any Colorado/Denver/Boulder frame or an unambiguously Colorado local entity such as Poudre School District, Broomfield, High Altitude Observatory, or Trail Ridge Road. The sign attaches to the whole formatted block, often at a space, comma, hyphen, parenthesis, or single digit. Ordinary dates, small counts, email-only contact labels, geographically nonspecific numbers, and any contact/citation inside a recognized Colorado local institutional frame are weak, unreliable, or positive under P2/P4. Negative for the capitalized label or adjacent token in an other-state natural-heritage program name such as “Alaska Natural Heritage Program” when it is outside a Colorado frame. This does not generalize to nature, wildlife, parks, outdoor recreation, rivers, mountains, or other-state geography: many such non-Colorado natural and geographical passages are positive or neutral. The cue is the program-label construction, not the topic of natural heritage.

examples.observed_prefix:
Putting pen to paper was once common and necessary, but in today's digital age the art of writing a letter is often lost. Modern technology simply can't touch the personal connection that a hand-written letter delivers. If you enjoy writing letters, or appreciate receiving hand-written letters in the mail then "Letters Home" is the perfect exhibit for you.
Letters Home explores Nevada's 160-year history through letters and correspondence written by the people who lived in and traveled to the state. The exhibit is on display now through December 2017 in the Special Collections & University Archives Department and throughout the third floor of the Mathewson-IGT Knowledge Center.
Exhibit curator Jessica Maddox came up with the idea to curate this exhibit as she was going about her job as an Accessioning Archivist in Special Collections.
"I picked up a letter, read it and thought 'wow!' there are so many things to learn about the people and history of our state by reading the letters we have in our collection," Maddox said.
From there she began working to bring the exhibit to life by identifying and pulling letters from more than 30 collections housed in the Department.
"People write letters for many reasons," she said. "By writing a letter individuals are able to illustrate the everyday occurrences that make a person or a place unique, convey their observations or impressions of where they are, describe the landscapes they see, and express feelings of loss to friends and relatives."
Letters on display cover a variety of themes including: landscape and weather, mining, ranching, business, everyday life, military, Native Americans, postage and the use of paper, and of course, vices.
The exhibit features the writing of several recognizable Nevadans. For example, letters between well-known journalist Joe McDonald and former United States Senator Pat McCarran highlight the struggle to determine whether or not McDonald's son had died in action during World War II. Through their correspondence, it was learned that McDonald was alive as a prisoner of war in China, and indeed not dead.
Other letters feature the writing of Mary Arrowsmith Evans, sister of John Newton Evans, and the name associated with the founding of the University of Nevada, Reno, Evans Ranch and Evans Avenue in Reno. Mary Evans took a railroad journey approximately six months after the Transcontinental Railroad was completed and wrote letters about her experience.
"Mrs. Evans was a widow when she hopped on a train in Defiance, Ohio and headed West," Maddox said. "The fact that she could do this and document what she saw when she stopped in Promontory, Utah and Reno is so important. She begins to tell the story of how her family was going to greatly impact the development of Reno."
Of all of the letters on display, Maddox does have a favorite.
"My absolute favorite letter is from the 1880s and it's a letter from a man on the Comstock writing about his desire to purchase a chicken," she said. "Who would have guessed that people living on the Comstock were also in the market for chickens?!"
All of the letters on display showcase the important historical documents housed in Special Collections.
When asked what she hopes people take away from the exhibit Maddox said, "Special Collections has materials to help the University and northern Nevada community make connections to the place in which we live."
She added, "Letters Home documents who we are and how we got to where we are as a state. What better way to demonstrate this by showcasing letters from the people who lived here and made history."
For information on "Letters Home" please contact Jessica Maddox via email at email@example.com or via phone at 775-68

The lack of any global warming over the last decade while carbon dioxide emissions have been increasing is extremely worrying to the global warming orthodoxy. Recently “peer-reviewed” papers have attempted to find excuses for this lack of warming. Sulphur emissions from coal plants in China it has been suggested have been cooling the earth! The effects of soot in the atmosphere have also been blamed for reality and measurements not corresponding to the (sometimes fanciful) results of climate models. Needless to say it would not be politically correct to accept that solar influences – through clouds for example – may be so powerful as to make any anthropogenic effects quite insignificant with regard to climate.
One school of global warming believers believe that the missing heat is being hidden like some Loch Ness monster in the deep oceans and will come back to haunt us in due course. Of course measurements can not find this “hidden” deep ocean heat. It is far too well hidden for that. But the “unhidden” measurable ocean heat content (upto a depth of 700m) also confirm the flattening out of global warming.
As Bob Tisdale had pointed out in WUWT: Global Ocean Heat Content Is Still Flat
Figure 1 is a time-series graph of the NODC Global Ocean Heat Content Anomalies from the start of the dataset (1st Quarter of 1955) to present (2nd Quarter of 2011).
Figure 1: Global Heat content
And as many are aware, Climate Model Projections of Ocean Heat Content anomalies did not anticipate this flattening. Figure 2 compares the ARGO-era (2003 to present) NODC Global Ocean Heat Content anomalies to the GISS Model-E Projection of 0.7*10^22 Joules per year. The linear trend of the observations is approximately 7% of the trend projected by the model mean of the GISS Model-E.
Figure 2 - Ocean heat content:measurements compared to models
But the heat cannot hide from the speculative computer models of our intrepid global warmers. And since they cannot find this heat they have instead programmed a super-computer to tell us that it exists and will appear again in a decade or two. A new paper entitled Deep oceans can mask global warming for decade-long periods is to be published online on September 18 in Nature Climate Change. The title itself illustrates the defense. The National Center for Atmospheric Research
